 Economics Reporter
 Show biography 
 In her role as Economics Reporter at The Telegraph, Emma Taggart is particularly interested in the labour market and monetary policy. She has previously worked at The Times and was the runner-up for young journalist of the year at the 2024 Scottish Press Awards. You can find her posting on LinkedIn and X @emmaftaggart
 Published 
 04 November 2026 6:00am GMT
 The annual cost of hiring a minimum-wage worker is poised to jump by more than £4,000 in just three years, analysis shows.
 The sharp rise in staff costs since Labour came to power follows a series of inflation-busting increases to the minimum wage, with the National Living Wage scheduled to rise by 3.9pc next year.
 Analysis by the Centre for Policy Studies (CPS) found that from April 2027, businesses will spend an additional £4,462 a year to employ a 21-year-old staff member on the minimum wage compared with 2024.
 The cost of hiring a worker on the National Living Wage for 35 hours a week will climb to £26,898 a year, up from £22,438 two years ago.
 At last week’s Budget , John Healey confirmed that the National Living Wage, which sets the minimum wage for those aged 21 or older, would rise from £12.71 to £13.21 per hour.
 However, Mr Healey also announced that the increase in the youth rate of minimum wage would be lower than in previous years, abandoning one of Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledges.
 Labour had promised to scrap what it called “discriminatory” youth rates in its election manifesto by raising them faster than the adult rate.
 However, employers have warned that the increase in the rates of minimum wage for under-21s and under-18s since Labour came to power has made it unattractive to employ younger workers.
 It comes as the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics showed that the unemployment rate for 16 to 24-year-olds was 15.6pc in the three months to August 2026, up from 13.8pc during the same period in 2024.
 Daniel Herring, the head of fiscal and economic policy at the CPS, said: “John Healey deserves some credit for slowing the rise in the youth minimum wage.
 “However, this Labour Government has continued to increase pressure on businesses during an incredibly difficult period for them.”
 Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, increased the minimum wage for 18 to 20-year-olds by 8.5pc to £10.85 per hour in April this year, more than double the increase for those aged 21.
 The increase in the youth rate of minimum wage means that the cost of employing an 18-year-old has risen by £4,859 a year between 2024 and April 2027.
 The rise in Mr Healey’s Budget means the youth rate will climb to £11.27, up by 3.9pc, the same pace as increases for those aged 21 and older.
 Mr Herring added that the Chancellor’s move to increase the National Living Wage “follows a decade of above-inflation rises in the cost of employing someone on the minimum wage”.
 Businesses left with no choice but to cut staff
 The cost of employing staff was also pushed higher in April 2025, when Labour raised employers’ National Insurance contributions, costing businesses an additional £26bn.
 Businesses have warned that increases to the minimum wage and taxes have left them with no choice but to cut staff numbers or freeze hiring.
 The latest figures from the Office for National Statistics show that the number of vacancies dropped to 691,000 in the three months to September, the lowest level since April 2021.
 A government spokesman said: “Our economy can only thrive when people have a wage they can count on, which is why we have raised the National Living Wage and National Minimum Wage to protect the real-terms value of the incomes of millions, without impacting on job opportunities.”
